name: Electoral Reform Society: proportional representation and UK democratic reform (charityevals)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: the UK's people, whose elections and Parliament the reforms change.
summary: The Electoral Reform Society campaigns for proportional representation for the House of Commons and for other changes to how the UK votes and is governed, from offices in London, Edinburgh and Cardiff ($3.0 million spent in 2024-25). It is a company limited by guarantee, not a charity, so gifts to it get no Gift Aid or tax relief; it is the only entity that takes donations, and this models it. A dollar is counted as doing what the average year of its 2016-2026 work did: its share of the reforms won or nearly won in that decade (the supplementary vote restored for England's mayors, the hereditary peers removed, votes at 16 across the UK and pilots of automated registration, now in the Lords, and the Welsh and Scottish franchise and Senedd acts), plus its share of an 8% chance, a campaign still pending, that the Commons is elected proportionally within ten years; each is valued as a small share of the income democracy brings (Acemoglu et al. 2019), built up over 25 years and repealed at 3% a year, and proportional representation gives about half of the result. With its next dollar at {{row:marginal_vs_past_average}} of the average, because it holds about 18 years of spending in its capital fund, that comes to about {{result}} years of healthy life per 1,000 dollars. The biggest uncertainties are whether a voting method changes how well people are governed at all and the chance of proportional representation, both judgments; every branch is discounted by the shared missing-data slider.

sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

People whose House of Commons elections a switch to proportional representation would change
rows.explainer: Everyone in the UK: Westminster's voting system covers every constituency.

rows.label: People in England who elect a mayor by the supplementary vote again
rows.explainer: England's people × the share living under an elected mayor once the new strategic authorities elect theirs in 2028. The English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act 2026 (Royal Assent 29 April 2026) returns mayors to the supplementary vote; police and crime commissioners are being abolished in 2028 (gov.uk, Police and crime commissioners to be scrapped, 13 November 2025), their powers passing to mayors, so no commissioner will be elected by it and Wales, with no mayors, is not reached.

rows.label: People in the UK whose elections votes at 16 would reach
rows.explainer: Everyone in the UK: the Representation of the People Bill lowers the voting age to 16 for all UK elections; the gain is counted per person governed, not per new voter.

rows.label: Scotland's 2020 franchise act against Wales's, per person
rows.explainer: The Senedd and Elections (Wales) Act 2020 and the Local Government and Elections (Wales) Act 2021 gave 16- and 17-year-olds and foreign nationals living in Wales the vote in Welsh elections; the Scottish Elections (Franchise and Representation) Act 2020 added only foreign nationals with leave to remain (16-year-olds had voted in Scotland since 2015, before the window). A Scottish resident gains about half (0.3 to 0.7) of what a Welsh one does: one group added of Wales's two, foreign nationals being a few per cent of the adult population, as 16- and 17-year-olds are.

rows.label: People in Wales and Scotland reached by the 2020 devolved franchise acts (Wales-equivalent)
rows.explainer: Wales's population plus Scotland's at its weight.

rows.label: People in the UK governed by Parliament without hereditary peers
rows.explainer: Everyone in the UK: the House of Lords (Hereditary Peers) Act 2026 (Royal Assent 18 March 2026, in force 29 April 2026) removed the 92 remaining hereditary peers.

rows.label: People in Wales who elect the enlarged Senedd
rows.explainer: Everyone in Wales: the Senedd Cymru (Members and Elections) Act 2024 enlarged the Senedd from 60 to 96 members, elected by closed lists in 16 six-member constituencies from 7 May 2026.

rows.label: People reached by the main campaign (proportional representation), for reading
rows.explainer: The main branch's reach, for reading; each branch has its own row.

rows.label: People released, cleared or kept out of detention in the year
rows.explainer: 0: the Society does no casework.

rows.label: Years of the Society's work the won reforms are counted against (2016-17 to 2025-26)
rows.explainer: The past average: the reforms won or nearly won in the ten years from April 2016 to March 2026 (the Welsh and Scottish franchise acts of 2020, the Senedd act of 2024, the hereditary peers and mayoral voting acts of 2026, votes at 16 in the Lords) against ten years of spending. The cost is always the ten years' average; the range 8 to 12 is about how typical the decade's wins are of the Society's record (no other reform it backed passed in 2014-2016, and wins cluster in some decades).

rows.label: Years for a governance gain to build up fully
rows.explainer: The shared build-up of democracy's income gain (25 years, 20 to 30).

rows.label: Years a won reform counts before it would have come anyway
rows.explainer: The site's one answer (docs/normalization.md 2.9).

rows.label: Discount rate plus the yearly chance a reform is undone
rows.explainer: The shared discount rate plus the shared repeal hazard (3% a year): mayors' supplementary vote itself was replaced by first past the post in 2022 and restored in 2026.

rows.label: Discounted full-effect years a won reform counts, its build-up brought forward
rows.formula: (1 - (1 + reform_rate) ^ (0 - years_of_impact)) * (1 - (1 + reform_rate) ^ (0 - ramp_years)) / (ln(1 + reform_rate) * ln(1 + reform_rate) * ramp_years)
rows.explainer: The family's shifted ramp: the gain builds over ramp_years from first use, and bringing the reform forward by years_of_impact moves the whole build-up earlier, at the shared rate plus the repeal hazard. Each branch multiplies it by its own wait.

rows.label: Share of democracy's income gain that proportional representation brings
rows.explainer: The shared figure ({{row:pr_gain_share}}, 1% to 15%), the share of a full switch of all of a resident's governments; the House of Commons' part is in pr_implementation_adj.

rows.label: Income gained per person per year under proportional representation, ln(consumption)
rows.explainer: ln(1 + democracy's long-run income gain × the share), at full effect.

rows.label: Proportional representation's own record against a contested issue's
rows.explainer: On a contested issue policy changes about 40% of the time within four years (@democracy.lobbied_issue_change_rate). This one is a constitutional change that the two parties that have won every election since 1945 gain from blocking, and the 2011 referendum on the alternative vote was lost by 68% to 32%; for it, Labour's 2022 conference backed PR, over 100 MPs sit in the parliamentary group on electoral reform, and the 2024 and 2025 results were the most disproportionate on record (Annual Review 2025); the horizon is ten years, not four. 0.2 (0.05 to 0.6) of the reference class.

rows.label: Chance the House of Commons is elected by proportional representation within ten years (a campaign still pending)
rows.explainer: One event: Parliament adopts a proportional system for general elections by 2036, the reference class times the issue's own record: {{row:pr_p_win}}.

rows.label: Years until a proportional-representation win, if it comes within ten
rows.explainer: A win somewhere in the next ten years: about midway, 5 (2 to 9); a referendum, as in 2011, would come first.

rows.label: Years until the first general election under proportional representation
rows.explainer: The wait for the win plus the shared wait from a win to the first election under the new system (2 years, 1 to 4).

rows.label: Discount for the wait, proportional representation
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Discounted full-effect years, proportional representation
rows.explainer: The shifted ramp after the wait.

rows.label: Probability of the win, proportional representation
rows.explainer: The chance of the win; the Society's part of it is its share of the movement's money (pr_attribution_share).

rows.label: Units of value of the proportional-representation win, before adjustments
rows.explainer: People × income gained × the value of a log point × the chance × the discounted full-effect years.

rows.label: The supplementary vote's effect against ranked-choice voting's
rows.explainer: The supplementary vote is a cut-down ranked ballot: two preferences, and only the top two candidates stay in the count, so second preferences for a third candidate are lost. In the 2000-2021 mayoral and PCC elections that used it, the second round decided most contests that went to it, as ranked-choice voting would. 0.6 (0.3 to 0.9) of ranked-choice voting's gain, the shared @democracy.rcv_gain_share.

rows.label: Share of democracy's income gain the supplementary vote brings, for all of a resident's elections
rows.explainer: The shared ranked-choice share (2%, 0.3% to 6%) at the supplementary vote's weight; the offices it covers are in sv_implementation_adj.

rows.label: Income gained per person per year, supplementary vote, ln(consumption)
rows.explainer: ln(1 + democracy's income gain × the share).

rows.label: Years from the act to the first elections under the supplementary vote
rows.explainer: Royal Assent 29 April 2026; the government meant the vote to be in use from 19 June 2026 (Electoral Reform Society, 30 April 2026, https://electoral-reform.org.uk/?p=9221). Most mayors, and all the new strategic authorities' first mayors, are next elected in May 2028: 2 years (1.5 to 2.2).

rows.label: Discount for the wait, supplementary vote
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Discounted full-effect years, supplementary vote
rows.explainer: The shifted ramp after the wait.

rows.label: Probability of the win, supplementary vote
rows.explainer: 1: the act is law; the Society's part is its share (sv_attribution_share).

rows.label: Units of value of the supplementary-vote win, before adjustments
rows.explainer: People × income gained × the value of a log point × the discounted full-effect years.

rows.label: Share of democracy's income gain that votes at 16 bring, for all of a resident's elections
rows.explainer: Votes at 16 add 16- and 17-year-olds, about 3% of the electorate, who turn out less than average but more than 18- to 20-year-olds where they have voted (Scotland's 2014 referendum, Austria). It changes who is heard more than who is elected. A tenth of a percent of democracy's gain (0.02% to 0.5%), a twentieth of ranked-choice voting's 2% (@democracy.rcv_gain_share), because a few per cent more voters move few seats, where a new count can change who wins any close race.

rows.label: Income gained per person per year, votes at 16, ln(consumption)
rows.explainer: ln(1 + democracy's income gain × the share).

rows.label: Chance the Representation of the People Bill's votes at 16 becomes law
rows.explainer: One event: the bill passed its Commons second reading on 2 March 2026 by 410 to 105 against a blocking amendment, finished its Commons stages in September 2026 (bill trackers) and is in the Lords. The reference class is a government bill with a majority behind it that has cleared the Commons, which nearly always becomes law, not a contested issue still being lobbied for (@democracy.lobbied_issue_change_rate); votes at 16 was in Labour's 2024 manifesto, so by convention the Lords don't block it, and the risk is delay to the end of the session. 90% (75% to 98%).

rows.label: Years until the first elections with votes at 16
rows.explainer: Royal Assent in 2027, then the English local elections of May 2027 or 2028 and the next general election by 2029: 2 (1 to 3).

rows.label: Discount for the wait, votes at 16
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Discounted full-effect years, votes at 16
rows.explainer: The shifted ramp after the wait.

rows.label: Probability of the win, votes at 16
rows.explainer: The chance the bill becomes law; the Society's part is its share (v16_attribution_share).

rows.label: Units of value of votes at 16 across the UK, before adjustments
rows.explainer: People × income gained × the value of a log point × the chance × the discounted full-effect years.

rows.label: Share of democracy's income gain that automatic registration, political-finance rules and wider voter ID bring
rows.explainer: The same bill gives powers to pilot automated voter registration ('piloted before introduction', Annual Review 2025), widens the accepted voter ID and tightens rules on political donations, 'all policies we have championed for years' (Annual Review 2025); Wales's Elections and Elected Bodies (Wales) Act 2024, which the Society backed, adds registration without application for Welsh elections. About 7 to 8 million eligible people are missing from or wrongly on the registers (Electoral Commission accuracy and completeness studies), but studies of access reforms find small changes in vote shares (Thompson et al. 2020 on postal voting). Half of votes at 16's share (v16_gain_share): 0.05% (0.01% to 0.3%), for the rollout the pilots lead to and the other rules.

rows.label: Income gained per person per year, registration and finance reforms, ln(consumption)
rows.explainer: ln(1 + democracy's income gain × the share).

rows.label: Discounted full-effect years, registration and finance reforms
rows.explainer: The same bill, so the same wait as votes at 16.

rows.label: Years until the registration and finance reforms take effect
rows.explainer: The same bill as votes at 16.

rows.label: Discount for the wait, registration and finance reforms
rows.explainer: The same bill as votes at 16.

rows.label: Probability of the win, registration and finance reforms
rows.explainer: The same bill as votes at 16 (the Welsh act, already law, is a small part).

rows.label: Units of value of the registration and finance reforms, before adjustments
rows.explainer: The UK's people × income gained × the value of a log point × the chance × the discounted full-effect years.

rows.label: The Welsh acts' franchise extension against votes at 16 alone
rows.explainer: The Welsh acts added two groups of about the same size, 16- and 17-year-olds and foreign nationals, where votes at 16 adds one: 2 (1.5 to 2.5, the foreign nationals perhaps fewer or less likely to register).

rows.label: Income gained per person per year, devolved franchise acts of 2020, ln(consumption)
rows.explainer: Votes at 16's share (v16_gain_share) for each group added, for the Welsh elections it covers; Scotland's one group is weighted in dev_people.

rows.label: Years from the 2020 acts to their first elections
rows.explainer: The Welsh act had Royal Assent on 15 January 2020 and was first used at the Senedd election of 6 May 2021 (1.3 years); Welsh councils followed in May 2022 (2.3 years). 1.5 (1.3 to 2.3).

rows.label: Discount for the wait, devolved franchise acts
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: Discounted full-effect years, devolved franchise acts
rows.explainer: The shifted ramp after the wait.

rows.label: Probability of the win, devolved franchise acts
rows.explainer: 1: both acts are law.

rows.label: Units of value of the 2020 devolved franchise acts, before adjustments
rows.explainer: People × income gained × the value of a log point × the discounted full-effect years.

rows.label: Share of democracy's income gain that removing the hereditary peers brings
rows.explainer: The Lords revise and delay laws but can't block the Commons for long; the 92 hereditary peers were about a ninth of the members who sit, and the rest stay appointed. A tenth of a percent of democracy's gain (0.02% to 0.5%), the same as votes at 16 (v16_gain_share): each changes who takes part in decisions at the margin, not who governs.

rows.label: Income gained per person per year, hereditary peers removed, ln(consumption)
rows.explainer: ln(1 + democracy's income gain × the share).

rows.label: Years from the act to its effect
rows.explainer: 0: the act removed the hereditary peers on 29 April 2026, a month after Royal Assent.

rows.label: Discount for the wait, hereditary peers
rows.explainer: No wait: 1.

rows.label: Discounted full-effect years, hereditary peers
rows.explainer: The shifted ramp.

rows.label: Probability of the win, hereditary peers
rows.explainer: 1: the act is law.

rows.label: Units of value of removing the hereditary peers, before adjustments

rows.label: Share of democracy's income gain a larger Senedd brings
rows.explainer: The Senedd grew from 60 to 96 members, which the Society backed: more members to scrutinise the Welsh Government. 0.3% of democracy's gain (0.05% to 0.8%), a seventh of ranked-choice voting's 2% (@democracy.rcv_gain_share). The same act moved it from the additional member system to closed lists, which the Society campaigned against (Annual Report 2024); that part is not the Society's work and isn't credited to it, either way.

rows.label: Income gained per person per year, Senedd reform, ln(consumption)
rows.explainer: ln(1 + democracy's income gain × the share).

rows.label: Years from the act to the first election under it
rows.explainer: Royal Assent in June 2024, first used at the Senedd election of 7 May 2026 (Annual Review 2025): 1.9 years (1.8 to 2).

rows.explainer: The shifted ramp after the wait.

rows.label: Probability of the win, Senedd reform
rows.explainer: 1: the act is law and was used in May 2026.

rows.label: Units of value of the Senedd reform, before adjustments
rows.explainer: People × income gained × the value of a log point × the discounted full-effect years.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, proportional representation
rows.explainer: The shared doubt that proportional representation changes how places are governed (0.6, 0.3 to 0.9); the shared gain shares are judged for rich democracies, so no further external-validity step applies. Studies across countries (Persson and Tabellini) link it to broader public spending; for national legislatures the evidence is cross-country, as uncertain as the US cities' record behind the fact.

rows.label: Share that wouldn't have happened anyway, proportional representation
rows.explainer: 1: $win_years_counted already says the reform would have come some day (Convention 5).

rows.label: The Society's share of the UK movement for proportional representation's money
rows.explainer: The share of the movement's money, Convention 2. The Society's England campaign spending was about £1.0 million in 2024-25 (staff £686,153 and campaigns £339,410), most of it for proportional representation; it is the oldest and largest UK group for it, with 18 staff. The others (Make Votes Matter, Unlock Democracy, Compass, the Labour Campaign for Electoral Reform, Fair Vote UK, the parties' own campaigners) are small companies or unincorporated groups that file micro-entity or filleted accounts without spending, most run by volunteers or a few staff, so their money can't be added up. Half (30% to 70%), a judgment.

rows.label: Years of the movement's campaign before 2026 a proportional-representation win rests on
rows.explainer: The campaign since the 2015 election (Make Votes Matter founded, the Society's renewed push): 10 years (5 to 20, counting from the 2011 referendum or earlier).

rows.label: Years of the movement's work a proportional-representation win is credited to
rows.explainer: The campaign so far plus the years until the win: one year of the Society's spending gets its share of the movement's money divided by these years.

rows.label: Credit for one year of the Society's work, proportional representation
rows.explainer: The Society's share of the movement's money over the years the win is credited to.

rows.label: This charity's share of the good done with money, work or budgets it brings in
rows.explainer: The site's one setting for resources another party commits only because of the organisation (docs/normalization.md 2.24): governments' budgets and enforcement, companies' compliance, the use others make of research. The charity is credited this share of the good done with them, net of their cost; the rest stays with those who paid or did the work. Fixed.

rows.label: Share of credit used: credit for one year of the Society's work, proportional representation
rows.explainer: The share among those who paid for or did the same work, times the mobiliser's share: the rest of the credit stays with those who carry out or adopt the result (docs/normalization.md 2.24).

rows.label: The House of Commons' share of a resident's governments above their council
rows.explainer: For the 84% of people in England the Commons is the only legislature above their council; in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland a devolved parliament, already elected proportionally, shares that level. 0.9 (0.75 to 1).

rows.label: Share of a full switch that the House of Commons brings
rows.explainer: The levels above local government (one minus the shared local share, 0.5) × the Commons' part of them.

rows.explainer: The shared doubt that ranked ballots change how places are governed (0.5, 0.25 to 0.85).

rows.explainer: 1: $win_years_counted already says the reform would have come some day (Convention 5).

rows.label: The Society's share among the campaigners for restoring the supplementary vote
rows.explainer: The Society's share among the campaigners. It opposed the 2022 switch to first past the post, argued for a preferential system before the bill was published and wrote to ministers after the May 2025 mayoral elections; the government announced the return in July 2025 ('We are delighted that the government listened', Annual Review 2025). Make Votes Matter and Unlock Democracy campaigned too. Anchor: the Society's judged share of the electoral-reform movement's money, about half (it spends about £1.0 million a year; the other groups are too small to file their spending). 50% (30% to 70%). The government and Parliament that made the change are under the mobiliser's share, not in this share; that the reform would have come some day is in the years a win counts.
